title: Evacuation Simulator
summary: An interactive agent-based model that lets students and humanitarians explore how information spread and demographics shape community evacuation behavior.

contribution.roleNote: Developed by Melanie MacKew as masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs (2026), under the Ethical Tech CoLab.

narrative.problem: In humanitarian evacuations, who leaves and when depends on how information spreads and on household demographics: alerts must be confirmed, neighbours influence one another, and elders, young children, pregnant people and unaccompanied minors move more slowly.
narrative.decision: Households are modelled as family clusters whose hub waits for every member, and each member must confirm an alert before milling begins; every transition from unaware to done is probabilistic and depends on threat level, info clarity and household composition.
narrative.tradeoff: Because transitions are probabilistic, a single run shows little and results need multi-run comparison; some outcomes, such as cars equalising vulnerability, follow directly from the parameter table rather than emerging from the model.
narrative.limitation: The independent peer review recommends major revisions and notes that no empirical output is reported: not a single run, figure or distribution.
narrative.caveat: A research prototype for academic demonstration and teaching only. Outputs are illustrative and are not a substitute for operational planning, legal advice, or assessment by qualified humanitarian and IHL professionals.
